questions.q: Why does the lesson describe pgvector as 'the closest thing to build' among the three options?
options: pgvector requires writing an entirely new database from scratch
It extends a PostgreSQL database the team likely already operates and understands, rather than introducing an entirely new specialized system -- closest to owning the infrastructure directly
pgvector cannot be used with PostgreSQL at all
pgvector is the most expensive of the three options
questions.explain: pgvector adds vector search directly inside existing Postgres infrastructure, meaning no new database system to adopt -- the build-vs-buy spectrum point closest to fully owning what's already there.

questions.q: Why does the lesson explicitly comment in the code that the scores are 'Northbeam's own judgment call,' not an objective universal ranking?
options: Because weighted scoring always produces exactly the same result regardless of the weights used
Because the weighted scores reflect this specific team's priorities and situation, and a different company with different priorities could legitimately score the same products differently
Because Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector are fictional products with no real characteristics
Because the scoring matrix technique from Lesson 8 cannot be trusted at all
questions.explain: This is the same honesty Lesson 8 taught about weights being a judgment call -- the scores here are specific to Northbeam's situation, and a team with different priorities (e.g., zero operational appetite) could reasonably reach a different, equally valid conclusion.

questions.q: In the worked scoring, Weaviate (7.50) narrowly beat Pinecone (7.40). What kind of DIFFERENT company situation might make Pinecone score higher instead, without Weaviate's win being 'wrong'?
options: No other company situation could ever produce a different ranking
The ranking is fixed and identical for every company regardless of their situation

A company with a smaller team and less appetite for operating any infrastructure might weight operational simplicity even more heavily, which would favor Pinecone's fully managed, zero-infrastructure model
Pinecone could only ever score higher if Weaviate stopped being open-source
questions.explain: The scoring reflects Northbeam's specific weights -- a team with even less operational appetite would weight 'operational_simplicity' more heavily, which could flip the ranking toward Pinecone's fully-managed model, and that would be an equally legitimate answer for that different situation.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the correct relationship between the weighted scoring matrix, the design document, and the ADR in this case study?
options: The scoring matrix, design document, and ADR are three unrelated, independent artifacts with no connection to each other
The ADR comes first and determines what the scoring matrix should conclude
The scoring and its reasoning become the Alternatives Considered section of a design document that drives the decision, which is then written down permanently as an ADR once approved
Only one of these three artifacts is ever actually necessary; the other two are redundant
questions.explain: This ties together the whole chapter: scoring produces reasoning, the design doc uses that reasoning to drive a decision (Lesson 9), and the ADR (Lesson 6) permanently records the decision once made.

questions.q: Why does the design doc propose starting with Weaviate's managed cloud offering rather than self-hosting it immediately?
options: It mitigates the real risk of operating a new system the team hasn't run before, deferring that operational step until the team has more experience with the product
This choice has no connection to any risk named in the design document
Managed cloud offerings are always permanently required and can never be changed later
Self-hosting Weaviate is technically impossible under any circumstances
questions.explain: This is a direct example of Lesson 9's 'Risks & Open Questions' discipline -- naming a real operational risk (an unfamiliar system) and proposing a concrete mitigation (start managed, self-host later once more experienced) rather than ignoring the risk.
